slides: Open by treating the chapter as a change of representation problem. Students already know many convex pictures, but this lecture asks what data makes those pictures testable: vertices, inequalities, support lines, incidence counts, and limiting approximations. Emphasize that the assigned PDF pages orient the topic, while the deck uses original diagrams and the notebook artifacts as the teaching spine.

Use the route to make a broad chapter feel navigable. The first contract is representation: do we know a convex set by its points, its vertices, or its supporting inequalities? The second is measurement: which formula is being approximated or checked? The third is stability: which conclusion survives when the object bends, refines, or approaches a smooth body?

Pause on the equivalence between vertices and half-spaces, because it is the workhorse behind the rest of the lecture. A picture of a polygon is not yet a mathematical object. Once students can name the vertex list and the inequalities, they can ask containment, support, area, and face questions without relying on visual guesswork.

Connect compactness to existence instead of treating it as a topological decoration. The support value is useful only because the maximum is attained, and the points of attainment form a face. For a polytope this face may be a vertex, edge, or facet; for a smooth body it may shrink to one point.

Use the generated hull image as a laboratory record. Ask students to point to the data that matters for the hull and the data that disappears from the boundary description. The interior points still explain the construction, but the finite certificate for many later questions is carried by the extreme vertices and their supporting sides.

Make area feel like a reproducible computation. The determinant formula is not merely a shortcut; it records orientation and lets the notebook compare polygons with a stable numerical convention. This prepares the regular polygon approximation, where the same signed-area machinery becomes evidence for convergence toward the disk rather than a one-off calculation.

Read the approximation from the table back to the image. The colored polygons are not a proof of the limit by themselves, but they tell students what the formula is measuring. The shrinking error column is the audit trail: as the number of sides doubles, the regular polygon better captures the disk while remaining finitely describable.

Separate geometry from combinatorics carefully here. Edge lengths, angles, and volumes can vary, but the incidence count remains stable for convex polyhedra with the same cell structure. The notebook JSON records small examples because they are enough to teach the invariant: tetrahedron, cube, and octahedron all land at the same value.

Use the Schlafli symbols to connect symmetry, incidence, and angle deficit. The inequality is a compact way to say that the faces can close around each vertex in positive curvature. It also explains why the list is finite in three dimensions, even though regular polygons in the plane form an infinite family.

Present Cauchy rigidity as a warning against flexible intuition. A paper model may wiggle when creased, but a closed convex polyhedron with corresponding congruent faces and the same incidence pattern has no such freedom. The proof idea tracks changes in dihedral angles and uses convexity to prevent the sign pattern that flexibility would require.

Stress that approximation is not a retreat from exact geometry. It is the bridge from smooth compact bodies to finite polytopes. Outer approximations remember support inequalities, while inner approximations remember sampled boundary points. The squeeze is powerful because many quantities, including area and support values, can be compared from both sides.

Treat isoperimetry as the chapter's global endpoint. Earlier slides asked how finite data represents, measures, and approximates convex objects. Here the question is extremal: among bodies with a fixed boundary measure, which one encloses the most? The polygon experiments make the circle and sphere feel reachable, while the inequality states the exact limit.

This activity is intentionally compact. It gives students one numerical approximation, one combinatorial invariant, and one support-face decision. Those three tasks mirror the chapter's main modes of thought. If time is short, do only the support question live and assign the area and Euler checks as a quick follow-up computation.

Close by asking students to name the data before naming the theorem. A convex hull, a support value, an Euler count, and an isoperimetric deficit are all ways of disciplining geometric intuition. The chapter is broad, but the recurring habit is simple: turn the object into a finite or limiting certificate, then check what remains invariant.
